Cities: Skylines dev: Don't punish your players; teach them
I agree with the sentiment, but sometimes punishments are necessary in games to prevent the player unknowingly screwing themselves over.
You've got a point. And some players just like to be beat up on a little bit if they make a wrong turn. I think there's a lot to be said about both approaches.

Yup! There's no "right way" as such, it just depends on the style of game. I would say Cities: Skylines benefits from teaching, whilst games like Dark Souls punish players for poor decisions, and are better games because of that.

If you read between the lines it's more about avoiding failure states than about reducing punishment. I'd say Cities: Skylines is not punishing enough though, especially for bad planning. In a sense it took way too much inspiration from the "build the city of your dreams despite violating every city planning rule ever" strand of games that everyone hated (SimCity: Societies probably is the worst offender).

But ultimately, avoiding failure states is why I like games such as Cities: Skylines or Mount & Blade Warband or even Dark Souls, but not Super Meat Boy. Failures don't carry any weight in SMB, you just try again. It's even quite contradictory with the idea of reducing punishment. In SMB, death is an absolute failure state: you lose everything and go back to the start of the level. It's "tolerable" because all the levels are so short. In that sense, the punishment for failure is nearly nothing: you go back to the start of a very short level. The punishment is a punctual loss of a tiny speck of progress. In a game that doesn't have such a strong failure state, you have to live with your past errors forever. A game that doesn't let you save scum (Dark Souls, EU4 or Warband on Ironman mode etc.) and forces you to struggle along or abandon your whole game is far more punishing than SMB. But also in my opinion far more rewarding. Actually being at risk of losing something valuable (your progress) gives meaning to the difficulty of a game. If failure isn't really a path that leads somewhere (see SMB), then failure doesn't actually exist.

That is a really good point! Games like BattleBlock theater punish you for dying, but on some levels I end up dying so often that it loses most of its meaning because I start to feel like if I just throw enough tries at a puzzle, I'll get it. I think punish vs teach has a lot more complexity than it appears at first blush.
